title: Glaciers and ice sheets
keyIdea: A glacier is a huge mass of ice made from snow. Where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer, the layers pile up and their weight squeezes old snow into firn and then hard glacier ice. The ice is so heavy that it slowly flows downhill. It grows when snow wins and shrinks when melting wins, but the ice still flows down. Rocks in the ice scrape river valleys into a U shape and leave piles called moraine. The ice sheets on Greenland and Antarctica hold enough water to raise the sea by about 65 m, and air bubbles in deep ice show what the air was like up to 800,000 years ago.
familyTip: Look at a photo or a map of a mountain valley, such as one in the Alps, Scotland or the Rockies. Is it a narrow V or a wide U? Then freeze a cup of water with a few layers of coloured ice and ask which layer froze first.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: bury snow until it turns to ice, balance snow and melt, carve a valley, melt ice into the sea, and drill an ice core.

kid: A glacier is a giant river of ice that moves very slowly. It does not come from a frozen river or lake. It starts as snow. In cold places high up or near the poles, more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. So each year a new layer of snow lands on top of the old one. The weight of the new snow squeezes the layers below. The snow grains join and the air is pushed out. After a year it is firn, which looks like wet sugar. After many years it is hard, blue glacier ice. For most glaciers this takes more than a hundred years.

Ice this thick is heavy, so it slowly flows downhill. If more snow is added at the top than melts at the bottom, the glacier grows longer. If more melts, the end moves back up the valley. But the ice itself still flows down. It just melts away faster than it arrives.

Rocks frozen into the ice scrape the ground like sandpaper. The ice also pulls out loose blocks of rock. A river cuts a narrow V, but a glacier fills the valley and leaves a wide U. When the ice melts, it drops piles of rock called moraine.

Greenland and Antarctica are covered by ice sheets, which are glaciers as big as countries. If all of Greenland's ice melted, the sea would rise about 7 m. Antarctica would add about 58 m. Sea ice already floats, so it hardly changes sea level when it melts. Deep down in an ice sheet, bubbles of old air show scientists what the air was like long ago.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This sits between KS2 geography (physical processes, the water cycle, polar regions) and KS3 glacial landforms. Key words: accumulation, ablation (melt), firn, glacier ice, mass balance, advance and retreat, abrasion, plucking, U-shaped valley, moraine, ice sheet, sea ice, sea-level equivalent and ice core.

Facts follow the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC). Snow that survives a melt season becomes firn, about two thirds as dense as water; continued burial squeezes out air until it is glacier ice, which for most glaciers takes more than a century. A glacier flows down and out under its own weight. Its mass balance (snow gained minus ice lost) decides whether the front advances or retreats. Greenland's ice sheet holds about 7.4 m of sea-level rise and Antarctica's about 58 m. The EPICA Dome C core holds about 800,000 years of trapped air.

Common mistakes: thinking a glacier is a frozen river or lake; thinking cold alone makes a glacier, when it needs snow to build up; thinking a retreating glacier flows backwards; thinking melting sea ice floods coasts, when only ice on land adds new water; mixing up the V of a river with the U of a glacier; and thinking deeper ice is younger.

In the lab your child buries snow until the first layer becomes ice, sets snow and melt to make a glacier grow, shrink and hold steady while a stone shows the ice still flowing down, carves a V-shaped valley into a U, melts three kinds of ice into the sea, and drills an ice core to put samples in age order.

practice.prompt: What is a glacier made from?
choices: Snow that piled up and was squeezed into ice
practice.hint: Think about what falls on a mountain each winter.
practice.explain: Snow. Layers of snow pile up and their weight squeezes the old snow into firn and then glacier ice.

practice.prompt: A glacier flows {a} cm downhill each day. How many centimetres does it flow in 10 days?
practice.hint: Multiply the distance each day by the number of days.
practice.explain: {a} cm × 10 days = {=a*10} cm. Glaciers move slowly, but they never stop.

practice.prompt: A glacier's end has moved back up its valley for 20 years. What is happening to its ice?
choices: It still flows down, but melts faster than it arrives
It is flowing back up the valley
practice.hint: Watch a stone sitting on the ice. Which way does it go?
practice.explain: It still flows down. The end moves back because the ice melts there faster than new ice arrives.

practice.prompt: Each winter {a} m of snow falls on a glacier and {b} m melts in summer. By how many metres does the snow pile grow each year?
practice.hint: Take away the melt from the snowfall.
practice.explain: {a} m − {b} m = {=a-b} m. More snow falls than melts, so the pile grows and the glacier can grow.

practice.prompt: Which shape does a glacier leave when it carves a valley?
choices: A wide U with steep sides
A flat plain with no sides
practice.hint: The ice fills the whole valley, not just the bottom.
practice.explain: A U. The ice scrapes the sides and floor, so the valley becomes wide and flat-bottomed with steep sides.

choices: Old snow that lasted a summer and is turning into ice
Ice that floats on the sea
pool.hint: It comes between fresh snow and glacier ice.
pool.explain: Firn is snow that lasted through a summer. It is denser than snow but not yet glacier ice.

pool.prompt: A freezing place gets almost no snow. Will a glacier grow there?
choices: No: it needs more snow to fall than melts
pool.hint: What is a glacier built from?
pool.explain: No. A glacier is built from snow. Without enough snow, there is nothing to pile up and squeeze into ice.

pool.prompt: A glacier gains {a} m of ice at the top each year and loses {b} m at its end. By how many metres does it gain each year?
pool.hint: Take the ice lost at the end away from the ice gained at the top.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} m each year. More is gained than lost, so the glacier grows.

pool.prompt: All the floating Arctic sea ice melts. What happens to sea level?
pool.hint: Is this ice on land or already floating in the sea?
pool.explain: It hardly changes. Floating ice already pushes aside its own weight of water.

pool.prompt: Which would raise sea level the most if it all melted?
pool.hint: Compare about 58 m, about 7 m and almost nothing.
pool.explain: Antarctica, about 58 m. Greenland would add about 7 m, and floating sea ice hardly any.

pool.prompt: Scientists drill an ice core in Antarctica. Where is the oldest ice?
pool.hint: Each year's snow lands on top of the last.
pool.explain: At the bottom. The deepest ice was buried first, so it is the oldest.

pool.prompt: Rocks frozen into a glacier scrape the valley floor. What is this called?
pool.explain: Abrasion. Rocks in the ice scrape and smooth the rock below, like sandpaper.

pool.prompt: A glacier's end moves back {a} m each year. How far does it move back in {b} years?
pool.hint: Multiply the distance each year by the number of years.
pool.explain: {a} m × {b} years = {=a*b} m. The end moves back, but the ice still flows downhill.
